evidenceScale.A: Strong: several good randomized trials or meta-analyses, used in dermatology guidelines
evidenceScale.B: Moderate: some randomized trials, consistent but smaller or shorter
evidenceScale.C: Weak: small trials, lab or mechanism data, mostly expert opinion

actives.name: Adapalene 0.1% (Differin)
actives.whatItDoes: An over-the-counter retinoid. It keeps pores from clogging, calms acne inflammation and slowly smooths texture. The gentlest retinoid that still works well on acne.
actives.howToStart: Pea-sized amount for the whole face on dry skin at night, 2-3 nights a week for 2 weeks, then every other night, then nightly if your skin is fine. Moisturizer on top. Skip it around the eyes and the corners of the nose and mouth.
actives.whenToExpect: Fewer new spots by 6-8 weeks; full effect at about 12 weeks. Acne can look a bit worse in weeks 2-6 (purging).
actives.sideEffects: Dryness, flaking, stinging for the first few weeks. More sun sensitivity, so SPF every morning.

actives.name: Retinol / retinal (OTC retinoids)
actives.whatItDoes: Cosmetic vitamin A. The skin converts it to retinoic acid. It speeds cell turnover and builds collagen over months. Weaker than prescription tretinoin; retinal (retinaldehyde) is a step stronger than retinol.
actives.howToStart: Start at 0.2-0.3% retinol 2-3 nights a week. Move up to nightly over 4-6 weeks, then to a stronger strength only if needed. Moisturizer on top if it stings.
actives.whenToExpect: Smoother texture in 4-8 weeks; fine lines and tone over 3-6 months.
actives.sideEffects: Dryness, peeling, redness while you adjust. More sun sensitivity.

actives.name: Tretinoin (prescription retinoid)
actives.whatItDoes: The best-studied anti-aging cream there is, and a strong acne treatment. It's pure retinoic acid, so it works faster and harder than retinol.
actives.howToStart: Prescription only: talk to a dermatologist. Usually 0.025% cream, pea-sized, 2-3 nights a week, building up to nightly over 4-8 weeks.
actives.whenToExpect: Acne: 8-12 weeks. Lines and tone: 3-6 months, still improving at a year.
actives.sideEffects: More irritating than adapalene: peeling, redness, stinging early on. Sun sensitivity.
actives.rxNote: Prescription only. Talk to a dermatologist (in person or telehealth).

actives.name: AHA (glycolic / lactic acid)
actives.whatItDoes: Water-soluble acids that loosen dead skin on the surface. Brighter, smoother skin and faster fading of marks. Lactic acid is gentler than glycolic.
actives.howToStart: A 5-10% leave-on (toner or serum) 1-2 nights a week, on nights with no retinoid. Go to 3 nights only if no stinging.
actives.whenToExpect: Smoother feel after a few uses; marks fade over 4-8 weeks.
actives.sideEffects: Stinging, redness, over-exfoliation if overused. More sun sensitivity for about a week after use.

actives.name: BHA / salicylic acid
actives.whatItDoes: An oil-soluble acid that gets inside pores and clears the gunk that makes blackheads. Mildly calming.
actives.howToStart: Easiest as a 2% cleanser once a day. As a leave-on (2% liquid), start 2-3 times a week on non-retinoid nights.
actives.whenToExpect: Fewer blackheads and less oil in 3-6 weeks.
actives.sideEffects: Dryness and peeling if overused. Avoid if you are allergic to aspirin.

actives.name: Benzoyl peroxide (BPO)
actives.whatItDoes: Kills acne bacteria and stops resistance to antibiotics. One of the strongest OTC acne ingredients. 2.5-5% works as well as 10% with less irritation.
actives.howToStart: Start with a 4-5% wash: on skin for 1-2 minutes, then rinse, once a day. Or 2.5% gel on acne areas. Body acne: a 10% wash in the shower.
actives.whenToExpect: Inflamed spots calm down in 2-4 weeks; best by 8-12 weeks.
actives.sideEffects: Dryness, peeling. Bleaches towels, pillowcases and shirts; use white ones.

actives.name: Azelaic acid
actives.whatItDoes: Calms acne and redness, kills acne bacteria and fades dark marks, including post-acne marks. Gentle enough for sensitive skin. 10% OTC; 15-20% by prescription.
actives.howToStart: Once a day (AM or PM) for 2 weeks, then twice a day if you want. Thin layer before moisturizer.
actives.whenToExpect: Redness and acne in 4-8 weeks; marks fade over 2-4 months.
actives.sideEffects: Brief tingling or itch in the first weeks that usually fades.
actives.rxNote: 10% is OTC; 15% gel and 20% cream are prescription (talk to a dermatologist).

actives.name: Niacinamide (vitamin B3)
actives.whatItDoes: An easy, low-risk all-rounder: less oil and redness, stronger skin barrier, slow fading of dark spots. 2-5% is plenty; 10% is no better and irritates some people.
actives.howToStart: Daily, AM or PM, in a serum or moisturizer. No ramp-up needed for most people.
actives.whenToExpect: Less oil in 2-4 weeks; tone and marks over 8-12 weeks.
actives.sideEffects: Rarely, flushing or a tingle at high strengths.

actives.name: Vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid and derivatives)
actives.whatItDoes: An antioxidant that adds to sunscreen's protection, brightens and slowly fades dark spots. L-ascorbic acid 10-20% has the most data but goes off quickly (turns orange).
actives.howToStart: A few drops in the morning before moisturizer and SPF. Start every other day if it stings. Keep it cool and closed.
actives.whenToExpect: Brighter tone in 4-8 weeks; spots over 3 months.
actives.sideEffects: Stinging, especially on fresh-shaved skin. Throw it out once it turns dark orange or brown.

actives.name: Sunscreen (broad-spectrum SPF 30+)
actives.whatItDoes: The highest-value step. It prevents sunburn, skin cancer, dark spots and most visible aging. It also protects the gains from retinoids and acids. Mineral filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) and chemical filters (avobenzone, octisalate, etc.) both work; pick the one you will wear every day.
actives.howToStart: Every morning, last step, about 2 finger-lengths for the face and neck (around 1/4 teaspoon), ears included. Reapply every 2 hours outside or after sweating. Scalp too if your hair is thin.
actives.whenToExpect: Prevention works from day one; spots stop getting darker within weeks.
actives.sideEffects: Some leave a white cast (mineral) or sting the eyes (chemical). Gel or fluid textures suit oily skin.

actives.name: Ceramides (barrier moisturizer)
actives.whatItDoes: Lipids that make up your skin barrier. Moisturizers with ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids repair dryness and make strong actives easier to tolerate.
actives.howToStart: Daily, AM and/or PM, as your moisturizer. Apply on slightly damp skin.
actives.whenToExpect: Less tightness in days; barrier repair over 2-4 weeks.
actives.sideEffects: Rare. Thick creams can feel heavy on oily skin; use a lotion.

actives.name: Hyaluronic acid
actives.whatItDoes: A humectant that pulls water into the top layer of skin. Skin looks plumper and feels less tight. Hydration, not treatment.
actives.howToStart: On damp skin, then seal with a moisturizer. Daily.
actives.sideEffects: Can feel tight in very dry air if not sealed with moisturizer.

actives.name: Tranexamic acid (topical)
actives.whatItDoes: Blocks one of the signals that tells skin to make pigment. Good for stubborn brown patches and post-acne marks; often paired with niacinamide or azelaic acid.
actives.howToStart: 2-5% serum once or twice a day. No ramp-up needed.
actives.whenToExpect: Visible fading from about 8 weeks; 3 months to judge it.
actives.sideEffects: Mild irritation now and then. (Oral tranexamic acid works better for melasma but is prescription-only with clotting risks: talk to a dermatologist.)

actives.name: Sulfur
actives.whatItDoes: An old, mild acne and dandruff ingredient. It dries out spots and calms them. Useful as a spot treatment or mask.
actives.howToStart: As an overnight spot treatment (e.g. a 10% lotion) or a 10-minute mask 2-3 times a week.

actives.name: Centella asiatica (cica)
actives.whatItDoes: A plant extract used in soothing products. Small studies suggest it helps redness and wound healing, but the evidence is thin.
actives.howToStart: In a moisturizer or serum, daily. Nice on days the skin feels raw from retinoids or shaving.
actives.whenToExpect: Calmer feel within days, if it helps you.
actives.sideEffects: Rare. Some cica products also contain fragrance or essential oils; check the list.

actives.name: Peptides
actives.whatItDoes: Short protein fragments that may signal collagen repair. Mostly lab and small industry-run studies; a nice extra, not a priority.
actives.howToStart: In a moisturizer or serum, daily.

actives.name: Topical clindamycin (prescription antibiotic)
actives.whatItDoes: Kills acne bacteria and calms inflamed spots. Must be used with benzoyl peroxide so the bacteria don't become resistant.
actives.howToStart: Prescription only: talk to a dermatologist, usually as a clindamycin + BPO gel, once a day. Not for long-term solo use.
actives.rxNote: Prescription only. Talk to a dermatologist.

am.note: Splash of water or a gentle wash.
Skip if your sunscreen is moisturizing enough.
SPF 30+, last step. Fluid or gel texture if oily.

pm.note: Gentle wash; gets sunscreen and sweat off.
Lotion if oily, cream if dry.

routines.name: Acne-focused
routines.description: The standard first-line plan from dermatology guidelines: benzoyl peroxide in the morning, adapalene at night.

am.note: 4-5% benzoyl peroxide wash, 1-2 min on the skin, then rinse.
SPF 30+, last step. Fluid or gel texture if oily.

pm.note: Pea-sized adapalene for the whole face, not just spots.
On top of adapalene to cut dryness.

routines.name: Oily skin + breakouts
routines.description: Keeps oil and clogged pores down without stripping the skin.

am.note: Niacinamide serum or a moisturizer that has it.
SPF 30+, last step. Fluid or gel texture if oily.

routines.name: Dry or sensitive skin
routines.description: Fix the barrier first. Add actives slowly, one at a time.

am.note: Rinse with water, or a cream cleanser.

pm.note: Azelaic acid 10% if you also have redness or spots; otherwise skip.

routines.name: Combination skin, texture and pores
routines.description: Retinoid most nights, a gentle acid on one night off.

am.note: SPF 30+, last step. Fluid or gel texture if oily.

pm.note: On 1-2 nights with NO retinoid: AHA or BHA leave-on.

routines.name: Dark spots and post-acne marks
routines.description: Sunscreen every day does half the work; the actives do the rest.

am.note: Tinted mineral SPF with iron oxides blocks visible light too, which helps pigment.

routines.name: Early aging and fine lines
routines.description: Sunscreen plus a retinoid: the two things with real evidence against aging.

am.note: With peptides or hyaluronic acid if you like.
SPF 30+, last step. Fluid or gel texture if oily.

pm.note: Retinol; or tretinoin from a dermatologist for stronger results.

routines.name: Redness and irritation
routines.description: Few products, no scrubs, nothing fragranced. Persistent facial redness with bumps may be rosacea: worth a dermatologist visit.

routines.name: Shaving bumps and ingrowns
routines.description: For bumps in the beard area: exfoliate gently and shave smarter.

am.note: Wash before shaving to soften hair.
SPF 30+, last step. Fluid or gel texture if oily.

pm.note: Salicylic acid or glycolic acid pads on the beard area.

conflicts.message: Retinoid and glycolic or lactic acid in the same night is a fast way to irritate your skin. Use the acid on a night off from the retinoid.
Retinoid plus salicylic acid leave-on in one night is a lot. Alternate nights. A salicylic wash in the morning is fine.
Retinol and AHA in the same session: split them onto different nights.
Retinol and BHA in the same session: split them onto different nights.
Tretinoin is strong on its own. Keep acids to other nights, or drop them.
Tretinoin and salicylic acid together tend to over-dry. Alternate nights.
Benzoyl peroxide can break down tretinoin. Use BPO in the morning and tretinoin at night (adapalene doesn't have this problem).
Keep benzoyl peroxide in the morning and retinol at night so they don't irritate together.
Vitamin C and an AHA together often sting. Vitamin C in the morning, acid at night.
Benzoyl peroxide oxidizes vitamin C. Use them at different times of day.
Two acids in one session is usually more exfoliation than you need. Pick one per night.
Two retinoids in one routine: pick one. They do the same job.
Adapalene and retinol are both retinoids. Use one.
Tretinoin replaces retinol; drop the retinol.
You started two new actives within 2 weeks. Add one at a time, 2-4 weeks apart, so you know what causes any irritation or breakouts.

guides.title: Starting Skincare as a Guy
guides.subtitle: The short version: wash, moisturize, sunscreen, then one treatment

sections.heading: What actually matters
sections.body: Most of what's sold as skincare is optional. Three things have real evidence behind them: daily sunscreen, a retinoid, and a moisturizer that keeps your barrier intact. Everything else is a nice extra.
bullets: Sunscreen every morning prevents most visible aging and dark spots.
A retinoid (adapalene OTC, or tretinoin from a dermatologist) handles acne, texture and lines.
Moisturizer makes the retinoid easier to tolerate.
A gentle cleanser beats bar soap, which tends to dry the face out.

sections.heading: Week 1 routine
sections.body: Morning: rinse or gentle wash, moisturizer, SPF 30+. Night: gentle wash, moisturizer. Do only this for a week or two so you know your skin is happy with the basics.

sections.heading: Adding a treatment
sections.body: Pick the one thing that bugs you most and add one active for it. Give it 8-12 weeks before you judge it.

rows: Azelaic acid; see a dermatologist if no better at 12 weeks
Salicylic or glycolic acid 2-3 nights a week

sections.heading: How much to use
sections.body: Retinoid: a pea for the whole face. Sunscreen: two finger-lengths for face and neck. Moisturizer: a nickel-sized dab. More retinoid does not work faster; it only irritates.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Starting five products at once.
Quitting a retinoid at week 3 because of dryness or purging.
Skipping sunscreen on cloudy days or when you're mostly indoors near windows.
Scrubbing with gritty exfoliants or hot water.
Fragranced aftershaves and colognes on the face.

guides.title: Purging vs. Breaking Out
guides.subtitle: Is the new product working or making things worse?

sections.heading: What purging is
sections.body: Retinoids and acids speed up skin turnover, so clogs that were already forming come to the surface faster. For a few weeks you can get more spots than usual. That's purging, and it means the product is working.

rows: Anything, often heavy creams, oils, sunscreens, hair products
New places you don't usually get spots
Small bumps, whiteheads, quicker to heal
Can be bigger, itchy, red patches or a rash
Keeps going as long as you use the product

sections.heading: What to do while purging
sections.body: Keep going, but slow the ramp-up (fewer nights a week), add moisturizer on top, and don't pick. If it's still worse at 8-10 weeks, it's not a purge.

sections.heading: When to stop
bullets: Itchy rash, swelling or hives: stop and switch products.
Spots in brand-new areas after a non-active product: drop that product.
Painful deep cysts or scarring: see a dermatologist; prescription treatment works and scars are easier to prevent than fix.

guides.title: Sunscreen Basics
guides.subtitle: The one product everyone should use

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: UV light causes most visible aging (lines, sagging, spots) and skin cancer. It also undoes the work of retinoids and acids and darkens acne marks. Daily sunscreen is the cheapest, best-proven step.

sections.heading: What to buy
sections.body: Broad-spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, water-resistant if you sweat. Mineral (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) and chemical filters both protect well; pick the one that feels good enough to wear every day.
bullets: Oily or acne-prone: gel, fluid or 'oil-free' labels.
Dry: lotion or cream.
Darker skin or dark spots: tinted mineral formulas avoid the white cast and add visible-light protection.
Bald or thinning scalp: spray or stick SPF on the scalp, or a hat.

sections.heading: How to apply
sections.body: About two finger-lengths for face and neck, ears included. Apply as the last morning step, about 15 minutes before going out. Reapply every 2 hours in the sun, and after swimming or sweating.

sections.heading: Myths
bullets: 'I don't burn, so I don't need it.' UV still ages and darkens skin of every color.
'SPF in my moisturizer is enough.' Only if you apply a full amount; most people use too little.
'Cloudy days don't count.' Most UV gets through clouds.

guides.title: Your Acne Plan
guides.subtitle: What dermatologists use first, and when to step up

sections.heading: Step 1: over the counter
sections.body: The first-line combo in the AAD guidelines: benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid. Adapalene 0.1% is OTC, so you can start today.
bullets: AM: 4-5% benzoyl peroxide wash, oil-free moisturizer, sunscreen.
PM: gentle wash, pea-sized adapalene for the whole face (ramp up over 6 weeks), moisturizer.
Optional: azelaic acid if you also have marks or redness.

sections.heading: Timeline
sections.body: Expect 8-12 weeks. Weeks 2-6 can look worse (purging). Take a progress photo every week in the same light; memory is a bad judge.

sections.heading: Step 2: see a dermatologist
sections.body: If it's not clearly better at 12 weeks, or you get deep painful cysts or scars, talk to a dermatologist. Prescription options are very effective.

rows: Strongly recommended for severe, scarring or stubborn acne; needs monitoring

sections.heading: Food and acne
sections.body: Evidence is mixed but leans one way: high-glycemic diets (lots of sugar, white bread, sweet drinks) and skim milk are linked to more acne in some studies, and a small trial found a low-glycemic diet helped. Whey protein shakes are a common trigger in case reports. People with acne also tend to have lower zinc. If you have acne, it's reasonable to try: fewer sugary foods, swap whey for casein or plant protein for 6-8 weeks, and see if it changes anything. Food is a helper, not a replacement for treatment.

sections.heading: Habits
bullets: Change pillowcases twice a week.
Wash after workouts.
Don't pick or squeeze; it makes marks last months.
Keep hair products (pomades, oils) off the forehead.

guides.title: Fading Dark Spots and Acne Marks
guides.subtitle: Sunscreen first, then the right actives

sections.heading: Types of marks
sections.body: Brown or dark marks after a spot heals are post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; they fade by themselves over months, faster with treatment. Pink or red marks are post-acne redness; they fade with time and calm skin, and acids help less. Indented marks are scars, which need procedures from a dermatologist.

sections.heading: The plan
bullets: Daily SPF 30+, tinted if you can. Without it, nothing else works well.
Azelaic acid once or twice a day.
A retinoid at night (also prevents new acne, so fewer new marks).
Optional: vitamin C in the morning, tranexamic acid or niacinamide serum.
Stop picking.

sections.heading: Timeline
sections.body: Brown marks usually fade noticeably in 8-12 weeks of treatment; deeper ones take 6-12 months. Melasma (symmetrical brown patches) is stubborn and relapses with sun; a dermatologist can add prescription options like hydroquinone, oral tranexamic acid or peels.

sections.heading: What to avoid
sections.body: Harsh scrubs, lemon juice, toothpaste and other DIY fixes irritate and can make marks darker, especially on medium and darker skin.

sections.heading: Before
sections.body: Shave after a shower or wash, when hair is soft. Use a shaving gel or cream; let it sit a minute.

sections.heading: During
bullets: Use a sharp blade; change it every 5-7 shaves.
Shave with the grain, light pressure, no going over the same spot again and again.
If you get bumps, fewer blades or an electric trimmer that leaves a little stubble helps a lot; very close shaves make curly hair grow back into the skin.
Rinse the blade after every stroke.

sections.heading: After
sections.body: Rinse with cool water, pat dry, then a fragrance-free moisturizer. Skip alcohol aftershaves. Don't put retinoids or acids on freshly shaved skin; apply them at night instead.

sections.heading: Razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis)
sections.body: Common with curly beard hair. Things that help: grow it out a bit, trim instead of shave, salicylic or glycolic acid 2-3 nights a week, never pluck ingrowns. If they keep coming back or leave dark marks, a dermatologist can prescribe options or discuss laser hair reduction.

sections.heading: Beard care
sections.body: If you keep a beard: wash it with your face wash, and use a little moisturizer or beard oil on the skin underneath. Flaky, itchy beard skin is often seborrheic dermatitis; a ketoconazole or zinc pyrithione wash 2-3 times a week usually fixes it.

guides.title: Actives Cheat Sheet
guides.subtitle: What each ingredient does and when to expect results

sections.heading: At a glance
sections.body: Evidence grades: A strong, B moderate, C weak.

rows: Smoother feel after a few uses
Fewer blackheads and less oil in 3-6 weeks
Inflamed spots calm down in 2-4 weeks
Calmer feel within days, if it helps you

sections.heading: Simple pairing rules
bullets: Retinoid at night, vitamin C and sunscreen in the morning.
Acids and retinoids on different nights.
Benzoyl peroxide in the morning if you use tretinoin.
Niacinamide, azelaic acid, ceramides and sunscreen go with almost anything.
